papers.title: CGDT-CESN: Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network for Multivariate Time-Series Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of multivariate time series requires models that simultaneously capture variable-specific dynamics and cross-variable interactions. In this work, a Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network (CGDT-CESN) is proposed, which comprises a modular reservoir architecture with each cluster distinctly specializing in one of the variables in the multivariate time series. An innovative reservoir design is proposed in which inter-cluster connections are enabled by empirically observed correlations among variables, providing a data-driven coupling mechanism. Apart from conventional readout training, inter-cluster connection weights informed by correlations are trained, which in turn allows the reservoir to capture time-varying cross-variable dependencies without sacrificing computational efficiency and further improves forecasting accuracy. The prediction performance of CGDT-CESN is found to be superior to that of the conventional ESN when evaluated on two fundamentally different datasets: Twitter information cascade evolution and solar wind forecasting. Also, the improvement in performance is preserved across multiple prediction horizons, even when presented with a low volume of data. By unifying cluster-specific specialization with learned inter-variable coupling, CGDT-CESN offers a principled, data-driven route to multivariate time series prediction.

papers.title: Noise-induced transitions between coexisting limit cycles beyond saddle-node bifurcations
papers.abstract: Nonlinear multistable systems with limit cycles may exhibit noise-induced transitions between oscillatory states, even in parameter regimes beyond the saddle-node bifurcations that determine the existence of these limit cycles. This behavior is associated with the ghost of a saddle-node bifurcation, a well-known feature of nonlinear systems near such bifurcation points. To investigate this phenomenon, we first consider a stochastic minimal model that supports two coexisting limit cycles within a parameter interval bounded by two saddle-node bifurcations. We numerically and theoretically estimate the probability of remaining near each stable attractor as a function of both the noise intensity and the distance to the ghost structure. The model is then extended by introducing spatially localized, non-homogeneous noise with enhanced intensity in a prescribed region of phase space. This modification is intended to emulate the asymmetric structure of the Hindmarsh-Rose model, in which bursting limit cycles approach each other closely in specific regions of phase space, thereby facilitating noise-induced transitions between them.

papers.title: When is vaccine prioritization worth optimizing?
papers.abstract: Optimizing vaccine prioritization is often treated as the default policy response when vaccine supply is limited. Yet optimized prioritization carries administrative, ethical and communication costs, motivating an upstream question: whether differences among vaccine allocations can alter epidemic outcomes enough to make optimization epidemiologically necessary. We show that optimization is not always worth pursuing: in some regimes, vaccination markedly reduces epidemic burden, but many feasible allocation rules perform almost equally well, making the necessity of optimization low. We quantify this necessity as the range of epidemic outcomes generated by different allocations under fixed supply and show that it is governed by competition between vaccinating high-contact groups to slow transmission and vaccinating groups that benefit most directly: necessity is low when these protection routes are balanced and high when one dominates. Increasing transmission intensity changes this balance and drives a transition in the optimal allocation from transmission-focused prioritization toward direct protection. Different prevention objectives exhibit distinct transition thresholds, creating regimes in which optimizing one objective substantially compromises another, thereby revealing when the choice of prevention target matters most. This framework reframes vaccine prioritization as a prior decision problem, identifying when optimization is warranted, when simpler rules suffice, and when prevention goals conflict.
